# The Old Night

Imagine waking at two in the morning in a farmhouse in the year 1650. The fire on the hearth has burned down to a bed of embers. Moonlight, when the clouds permit it, comes through a horn-pane window in a colorless wash. Somewhere a dog is barking, then stops. You are lying in a bed you share with two of your children, and your husband or wife is beside you, breathing slow. And you are wide awake—alert, calm, maybe even cheerful. No one in the house finds this strange. No one in the village would. The night is not one long block of unconsciousness. It has rooms in it, and you have just walked from one into the other.

For almost the entirety of human history, this is how people slept: in two installments. The historian Roger Ekirch stumbled onto this fact in the archives, where he kept tripping over a phrase that no one ever bothered to explain: *first sleep*. It appeared in depositions and diaries, in medical treatises and sermons, in plays and novels, across five centuries and several languages. Homeric heroes fall into first sleep. Chaucer mentions it. So does Cervantes, and so does Dickens. The phrases *first sleep* and *second sleep* were as unremarkable to their readers as *breakfast* is to us—so unremarkable that when Ekirch finally published his findings in 2005, in a book called *At Day's Close*, the discovery landed like an archaeological bomb. He had collected, by his count, more than five hundred references to the segmented pattern, and not one of them needed a footnote. Everyone knew. We had simply forgotten.

Then the physiological evidence arrived, almost by accident. In the early 1990s, a researcher named Thomas Wehr at the National Institute of Mental Health ran an experiment on the psychology of darkness. He sequestered volunteers and gave them fourteen hours of darkness every night for a month—no lamps, no screens, nothing to do but rest from dusk until dawn, roughly the light budget of a winter in a pre-industrial village. At first the subjects just slept long, as if repaying a debt. But by the fourth week something more interesting happened. Their sleep split in two. They would fall asleep for three or four hours, wake quietly for an hour or two in the middle of the night, and then sink back down until morning. And the middle hours were not tossing insomnia. They were marked by a distinctive calm, an endocrine state unlike ordinary wakefulness—prolactin elevated, minds placid, a little like meditation. When the electric lights came back, the two sleeps fused into one and the interval vanished.

Ekirch has argued, persuasively, that this old rhythm still surfaces in us, and that it may be hiding inside one of modern medicine's most common complaints: middle-of-the-night waking, the kind doctors call sleep maintenance insomnia. If you wake at three and lie there in the dark calculating your remaining hours with mounting dread, you may not be broken. You may be punctual—keeping an appointment your ancestors kept for thousands of years, an appointment that electric lighting quietly deleted from the calendar without telling your body.

What did people do with the interval? Ekirch found that it had a name in some places—people called it "the watch"—and a whole culture around it. It was the hour for prayer; many of the faithful believed God's attention was particularly available at that depth of night. It was the hour for small work: stoking the fire, checking the child, fetching a posset, perhaps stepping out to converse with a neighbor who had also woken, two pale figures talking across a fence under a full moon. Physicians of the era actually recommended this as the best time for a couple to make love—warm, rested, unhurried—and some advised couples who wanted children to schedule accordingly. Above all, it was the hour for dreams. Waking naturally between sleep cycles means waking directly out of them, and pre-modern people lay in the dark for an hour mulling what the night had delivered: warnings, visits from the dead, hints from God, news of sailors. Dreams were correspondence, and the watch was when you opened your mail. The French even had a word for the state of mind the interval produced—*dorveille*, a hovering between sleeping and waking in which visions were thought to be especially likely. The state has a romantic history. The modern equivalent is a phone screen in a dark bedroom, and the visions are other people's vacation photos.

The old night around those two sleeps was a place, not an absence. And it was expensive to light. Economists who have traced the history of artificial light estimate that at the dawn of the nineteenth century, an hour of reading by candle cost the equivalent of many hours of labor—orders of magnitude more than the same light costs now. Ordinary households lived by firelight, and by the moon. A rushlight—a dried rush dipped in kitchen fat—guttered out in minutes and smelled like a frying pan. Tallow candles smoked and stank; beeswax belonged to churches and the rich; whale oil was for those who could afford the sea in a bottle. The word *curfew* is just this economy fossilized into law: from the French *couvre-feu*, "cover the fire," the bell that William the Conqueror ordered rung to tell English households to bank their flames. When the moon was full, people worked by it—there were moonlight harvests, and the autumn "harvest moon," which rises soon after sunset for several evenings running, was not a poetic flourish but a paycheck, extra shifts of light granted by the geometry of the sky.

Sleep itself was communal in ways that would strike us as outrageous. Strangers shared beds at inns as a matter of course, and travelers complained less about the arrangement than about the particular snoring of their bedfellows. Children slept together, lodgers slept in the family's room, the boundary between sleeping bodies was a social one, not a physical wall. Night privacy—the expectation of an unshared bed, an unshared hour—is a modern invention, roughly as old as the middle class.

And the old night had its own government, its own dangers, its own liberties. It was feared, sincerely. The dark was where footpads waited on the heath and where the dead walked; belief in apparitions was not a superstition to be embarrassed about but a serious possibility, occasionally entered into court records. People believed night air itself was noxious—miasma, the bad breath of the world—and sensible households sealed their windows against it; as late as the 1860s, Florence Nightingale was still having to argue that "night air," a phrase spoken with dread, would not actually poison you. Yet darkness also concealed. Under its cover, servants slipped out, apprentices rested from their masters, enslaved people fled, lovers met, Catholics heard mass in attics, and the poor gathered where no daylight authority could see them. Night was the other country, with different laws and different citizens, and everyone crossed the border nightly whether they wished to or not.

Then we built lamps, and then we built lamps that fed on wires. Gas arrived first: in 1807, Londoners watched a stretch of Pall Mall glow for the king's birthday, and within a generation the gas companies had threaded every major city with pipes, turning the streets into chandeliers. Edison's practical bulb followed in 1879, and by 1882 a single power station in lower Manhattan was lighting a square mile of it. What followed was less an invention than an annexation. Night became profitable. Factories ran shifts around the clock; newspapers went to press at dawn fresh from the linotype; the night shift was born, along with its necessary civilization of diners, streetlights, police beats, and late trains. Cities advertised their glow. The phrase "the city that never sleeps" was a boast. Nobody much noticed that the other country had been occupied and its border erased.

The two sleeps thinned out of the record during exactly these decades, which is the strongest circumstantial evidence we have: as artificial light spread, the references to *first sleep* dried up, and by the early twentieth century the phrase was so dead that scholars initially assumed it had always been a metaphor. In the 1960s, anthropologists working among the Tiv of Nigeria—a people then still living without electricity—heard witnesses casually date events to "first sleep" and "second sleep," as if reporting from the seventeenth century. The pattern was never lost by humanity. It was lost by lighting.

The starliest casualty, though, was not in our beds. It was overhead. We tend to imagine that pre-modern nights were simply dark, but that's our poverty talking. The old night was full—a moving, glittering, legible vault. The Milky Way arched over every village on Earth, plain as a river. The sky was humanity's oldest calendar: the Pleiades rising at dusk to announce planting seasons that Hesiod was already writing down nearly three thousand years ago; Sirius appearing at dawn to warn Egypt that the Nile was about to flood. It was the oldest map: Polynesian wayfinders holding star paths in their heads across thousands of miles of open ocean; Harriet Tubman walking north by the North Star, for which, for some, the night was not a mystery but a compass needle and a door. It was the oldest screen, too—every culture on Earth has projected its families, its quarrels, and its animals onto the same scatter of stars, so that a Greek shepherd and a Navajo grandmother, separated by an ocean and a millennium, looked up at the Pleiades and both saw seven sisters.

We do not see it anymore. In January 1994, an earthquake knocked out the power across Los Angeles, and in the strange silent dark afterward, people began calling police stations and the Griffith Observatory to ask, some of them anxiously, about a vast silvery cloud that had appeared in the sky. The operators had to explain that the ominous thing was the Milky Way—our own galaxy, the combined light of a couple hundred billion suns, which had been hanging over those neighborhoods all along and had simply been outshone. By the most careful census yet taken, some eighty percent of North Americans and about a third of all human beings now live under skies where the Milky Way is invisible. We are the first generations in the history of the species for whom the night sky is blank. And our eyes know what we're missing: fully dark-adapted vision takes half an hour to arrive, the rods slowly filling with their light-sensitive dye, and a single glance at a bright phone screen undoes much of it. We carry equipment built over millions of years for the old night, and almost never take it out of the box.

The costs are not only aesthetic. Sea turtle hatchlings hatch at night and crawl toward the brighter horizon, which for fifty million years has meant the seaward glow; a beachfront now means they march inland toward the highway lamps. Migrating birds navigate by skies that we have rewritten, and researchers studying the Tribute in Light beams over Manhattan found them gathering more than a thousand birds at a time into exhausted circling—the lights now have to be doused in intervals just to let them disperse. Moths spiral into fixtures in a fatal obedience; fireflies, who find each other by their own small lights, are going quiet in the glare; whole insect populations measurably thin where the nights are brightest. And we are not exempt: light at night—especially the blue-rich kind—suppresses melatonin and scrambles the circadian clock, and the World Health Organization's cancer agency classifies shift work that disrupts circadian rhythm as a probable carcinogen. The occupation of the night has a body count.

But there is a subtler loss, harder to tabulate. When night became a mere appendix of day—dimmer, but continuous with it, same errands, same screens—we lost a boundary that human minds used to cross twice a day. There was a threshold, and crossing it changed what kind of thinking happened. On the far side were dreams taken seriously, an hour of unhurried lying-in-the-dark conversation, the strange thoughts that only arrive in *dorveille*. Now the threshold is gone; the day flows through the night without meeting any resistance, and we wake from dreams mid-sentence to alarms, with no interval to read what the night left us.

None of this argues for smashing the lamps. A lit street is a mercy for anyone walking home alone; a lit NICU is one of the moral triumphs of the species; some of the best things humans do happen under electric light at hours when our ancestors were asleep in their smoke. The argument, rather, is for restoring the border, at least occasionally, on purpose. That impulse now has an infrastructure: a movement begun in 1988 by a physician and an astronomer, which has since certified dark-sky parks and reserves around the world, places where the old night has been re-established by treaty and careful lamplight. You don't strictly need one. You need a new-moon night, a place with less sky glow than you think you have, half an hour of patience, and the discipline to not check the phone. Veteran watchers of the darkest deserts swear that under the very best conditions the Milky Way is bright enough to cast the ghost of a shadow.

And the waking hour is easier to recover than the stars. The next time you surface at two or three in the morning, consider that you may not be suffering from anything. Lie in the dark. Don't do arithmetic about the morning. Let the mind do what it did for a thousand generations in that hovering hour—drift, remember, make odd connections, half-dream without the drug of the screen. Often, the second sleep will simply arrive, exactly as it did for the farmhouse sleeper in 1650, and carry you back under.

We spent a few brilliant centuries convincing ourselves that darkness was merely the absence of light, a hole where day had failed, and so we filled it in. It never was. Darkness was a room of its own—full of stars and dreams and danger and rest, a different physics for thinking in. We sealed the door from our side, out of what is, honestly, a reasonable fear of the dark.

The good news is that the lock was on the inside all along.
